lines.text: אוה 21 אול
Piel. אִוָּה i. q. Kal no. 2, to desire, to
long for, ascribed mostly to the soul, נֶפֶשׁ.
Prov. 21, 10 נֶפֶשׁ רָשָׁע אִוְּתָה רָע the soul
of the wicked desireth evil. Deut. 12, 20.
2 Sam. 3, 21. Mic. 7, 1. Without נֶפֶשׁ
בַּלַּיְלָה my soul even I desire thee in the
night; comp. עַבְדְּךָ for I, with 1 pers.
Hithpa. הִתְאַוָּה, fut. apoc. יִתְאָו Prov.
23, 3. 6, i. q. Pi. but pr. to desire for one-
self, to long; absol. 1 Chr. 11, 17; c.
acc. Deut. 5, 18. Jer. 17, 16; c. dat. Prov.
23, 3. 6. הִתְאַוָּה תַּאֲוָה to long a longing,
i. e. to long for with eagerness, to lust
after, Num. 11, 4. Ps. 106, 14. Hithpael
differs also from Piel, in that it is never
joined with נֶפֶשׁ, which is the common
usage with Piel.
Deriv. אַו constr. אוֹ, אַוָּה, אֲוִי, אִי I,
תַּאֲוָה, מַאֲוַיִּים.
* II. אָוָה obsol. root, onomatopoetic,
to cry, to howl, ululare; so Arab. عَوَى
to howl, as a dog, wolf, jackal; see the
deriv. אוֹי, אִי.
* III. אָוָה, in Kal. not used, prob.
to sign, to mark, to describe with a mark;
kindr. with תָּאָה and תָּוָה. Comp. אָבָה,
אָוָה I, תָּאַב, to desire. Hence
Hithpa. id. Num. 34, 10 הִתְאַוִּיתֶם לָכֶם
ye shall mark out for yourselves a border,
etc. comp. v. 7. 8, where in the same
connection is read fut. תְּתָאוּ לָכֶם. Sept.
and Syr. in all three passages, καταμε-
τρήσετε, ܬܬܡܫܚܘܢ, ye shall measure out,
determine.—Hence also אוֹת for אָוֶת, a
sign.
אַוָּה f. (r. אָוָה I. 2) 1. desire, long-
ing, e. g. after food, with נֶפֶשׁ, Deut. 12,
15. 20. 21. 18, 6; of sexual desire, Jer.
2, 24. Comp. in אָוָה I. Pi.
2. desire, pleasure, will, with נֶפֶשׁ,
1 Sam. 23, 20; simpl. Hos. 10, 10.
אוּזַי (prob. i. q. אֻזִּי, עֻזִּי, strong, ro-
bust) Uzai, pr. n. m. Neh. 3, 25.
אוּזָל Gen. 10, 27, pr. n. Uzal, a de-
scendant of Joktan, here taken in a geo-
graphical sense for a city and district of
the Joktanidæ in Arabia, prob. the same
afterwards called Sanaa, the metropolis
of the kingdom of Yemen; see Bochart
Phaleg. II. 21. J. D. Michaelis Spicil.
Geogr. Heb. ext. T. II. p. 164 sq. Rut-
ger’s Hist. Jemanæ, p. 217.
אֱוִי (desire or dwelling, i. q. אַוִּי) Evi,
pr. n. of a king of Midian, Num. 31, 8.
אוֹי (r. אָוָה II) 1. Subst. wailing,
lamentation. Prov. 23, 29 לְמִי אוֹי לְמִי
אֲבוֹי who hath wailing, who hath want?
2. Interj. wo! a) Of sorrow, grief,
c. dat. wo to me! etc. 1 Sam. 4, 8. Is.
3, 9. 6, 5; rarely c. acc. Ez. 24, 6. 8;
absol. Num. 24, 23. b) Of threatening,
imprecation, Num. 21, 29.—Kindr. is הוֹי.
אוֹיָה i. q. אוֹי, c. dat. Ps. 120, 5.
אֱוִיל m. (r. אָוַל) plur. אֱוִילִים 1. fool-
ish, as adj. אִישׁ אֱוִיל Prov. 29, 9. Hos.
9, 7. More freq. subst. a foolish man, a
prudent man (עָרוּם) Prov. 12, 16; to a
wise man (חָכָם) Prov. 10, 14.
2. Impl. impious, wicked, Job 5, 3.
אֱוִילִי id. with adj. ending, foolish,
אֱוִיל מְרֹדַךְ Evil-Merodach, pr. n. of
a king of Babylon, who set at liberty
Jehoiachin king of Judah after he had
been long detained in prison by Nebu-
chadnezzar, 2 K. 25, 27. Jer. 52, 31. He
succeeded Nebuchadnezzar, and reigned
two years, according to Berosus in Jos.
c. Ap. 1. 20.—As to the signification of
the name, מְרֹדַךְ q. v. is the name of a
Babylonish idol, and אֱוִיל is in Heb. fool-
ish. But we may take it for granted
that some other name of Assyrian or
Persian origin lies concealed under this,
which the Jews thus wrested into the
analogy of their own tongue; pleasing
themselves perhaps with the idea of
calling the hostile and gentile king in
scorn Merodach’s fool, i. e. his foolish
worshipper.
* אָוַל with Vav movable, obsol. root,
i. q. יָאַל, יָאַל, to be foolish, pr. to be
turned away, perverse, comp. kindr. עָוַל,
and also אוּל. Hence אֱוִיל, אֱוִילִי, fool-
ish, אִוֶּלֶת folly.
* אוּל and אִיל a root not used in

line_status.note: Holem is printed over the vav (אוֹ), not the aleph; third item has ḥaṭeph-pataḥ under aleph and no dagesh in vav (אֲוִי), as Reading B has it.
The second word's first letter has the same form as the first letter of תָּאָה — a tav with a left foot and a dagesh — not a he; so תָּוָה (Reading A) is printed, not הָוָה.

The Hebrew is identical in both readings and matches the print (הִתְאַוִּיתֶם with dagesh + hiriq in the vav, plene yod; לָכֶם). The only difference is the stem label: it is printed with a full-size capital H followed by small capitals ("Hɪᴛʜᴘᴀ."), which B's mixed-case "Hithpa." represents; A's all-caps loses the initial-capital/small-cap distinction.

The Syriac word after the two taws clearly shows mem, shin, ḥeth, waw, nun (root ܡܫܚ "measure", Ethpaal 2mpl ܬܬܡܫܚܘܢ); Reading A's ܬܬܚܡܘܢ drops the mem–shin and reverses the order. No Syriac points are printed.

Second Hebrew word: under the alef is a qamets (horizontal bar with a stem), not a hiriq dot, and under the vav a cluster of dots (segol), not a simple two-dot sheva — matching Reading A (אָוֶת). A small dot sits above the vav in the print, apparently a stray mark/ink spot rather than a holem, so not transcribed.

Printed order after "i. q." is aleph-form then ayin-form (B's order, not A's), but the aleph-form is pointed exactly like עֻזִּי — qubuts under aleph, dagesh in zayin, hiriq — not אֲזַי as B gives; so A has the vowels right but the order wrong, B the order right but the vowels wrong.

The word after "i. q." ends in a yod before the closing parenthesis (not bare אַו), and a dot is printed in the vav (dagesh) with patach under the aleph — matching B's אַוִּי. Reading A drops the final yod.

Under the dalet the print shows a flat horizontal stroke with no descending stem — a patach (דַ), not a qamets (דָ). This matches the standard pointing מְרֹדַךְ (Jer. 50:2). Reading A is correct; Reading B's qamets is not what is printed.
